newsitem.title: USA: US Energy Dept warns on computer program AOL4FREE.
newsitem.headline: US Energy Dept warns on computer program AOL4FREE.

text.p: U.S. Energy Department's Computer Incident Advsiory Capability team issued a strong warning Thursday on a computer program called AOL4FREE.
Attempting to distinguish hoaxes from truly dangerous computer programs and viruses, the CIAC said the AOL4FREE program originated as a way to fraudulently create free accounts on America Online.

But a new version of the program, 993 bytes in length, is programmed to erase a user's hard drive, CIAC said. The team issued the alert to its global mailing list and posted a warning on its web site http://ciac.llnl.gov.
Simply downlaoding or reading an email message containing the rogue program would not cause damage, CIAC said. A user would have to run the program to cause damage.
The warning followed an erroneous warning being circulated on the Internet about AOL4FREE, CIAC said.

"That warning is either a hoax or a badly misunderstood description of this Trojan Horse," CIAC said. A Trojan Horse program, referring to the horse of Greek mythology, appears to be a legitimate piece of software, but performs another function when run, such as erasing a user's hard drive.
The CIAC is sometimes overwhelmed with reports circulated on the Internet warning of computer viruses, many of which turn out to be hoaxes.
Notable examples of hoax warning posted on CIAC's web site at http://ciac.llnl.gov/ciac/CIACHoaxes.html include "Goodtimes", "Irina" and recently "Penpal Greetings."
The anonymous warning about AOL4FREE, which said reading an email message containing the program could cause damage, was just such a hoax, CIAC said.

"CIAC still affirms that reading an email message, even one with an attached program, can not do damage to a system," the group said. "The attachment must be both downloaded onto the system and run to do any damage."

Based at Lawrence Livermore Laboratory in Livermore, California, the CIAC responds to computer security incidents at the Department of Energy and its contractors. The group issues periodic warnings about viruses, vulnerabilities in commercial software and other computer security issues.
